attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his own post, written in his voice.

semantics.note: The 'when the market works that out' trigger is kept as the antecedent. The scope (every public software company, many hardware ones) and the firm 'will' are preserved. 'Hit hard' is a fair rendering of 'hell to pay'.

contract.note: The contract reads 'other ways' as growth beyond generative AI, requires documented market recognition, and keeps the universal software scope. This is an ordinary reading. It invents no threshold or deadline.

evidence.note: MSCI documents an industry-wide software repricing in early 2026. It attributes this to AI disruption of software, not to recognition that the four named firms lack other growth avenues.
MSCI calls the July 2026 drop a crowded-trade unwind, not a reassessment of AI growth. So the antecedent was not met by that episode.
A secondary report of a general reassessment of AI returns in October 2026. It does not document the specific market recognition the antecedent requires.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows the market recognising that Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta have no growth avenues beyond generative AI. The software selloffs it describes are attributed to AI disruption or position unwinds. Because the antecedent is unknown, the policy says the claim is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. 'As I wrote before' refers to his own earlier writing, not to someone else.

semantics.note: The scope 'the rest of the generative AI industry' is restored. In context, the projections are OpenAI's revenue projections, so the wording is faithful.

contract.note: The plain reading is that OpenAI overwhelmingly dominates and competitors offer no credible revenue basis for its projections. That reading is ordinary. Choosing Q1 2025 is the evaluator's decision, but a reasonable one. The result depends on how much competitor activity counts as 'suggesting' a revenue base.

evidence.note: A court finding shows ChatGPT with a large lead in daily queries (March 2025) next to substantial rival activity. These are usage figures, not revenue, and partly OpenAI's own estimates.
A reported annualised revenue figure for Anthropic shows a growing business outside OpenAI. It is a run rate, not realised revenue, and does not test OpenAI's projections.

reviews.rationale: The usage data fits OpenAI's dominance, but the packet has no comparable revenue figures for the industry in Q1 2025. Anthropic's growth shows some outside commercial activity, but neither item settles whether the rest of the industry gave a credible revenue base for OpenAI's projections. The evidence does not decide the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: All four parts (hallucinate, expensive, unreliable, do little) are kept as present-tense observations about the models of the time.

contract.note: Reading 'don't do much' as limited useful task capability, not literally nothing, is fair and ordinary. Assessing each part separately is appropriate. The April 2025 window is the evaluator's choice but reasonable.

evidence.note: OpenAI's April 2025 system card reports substantial hallucination rates on SimpleQA and PersonQA. It is the developer's own disclosure, but it admits a weakness. Supports the hallucination part and the factual-unreliability part.
GPT-4.1 resolves 54.6% of SWE-bench Verified tasks, which cuts against 'don't do much'. This is a benchmark the developer reported itself, with some problems omitted.
Epoch shows API prices falling, using data from before the April window. Prices are not operating costs, so this does not settle the expense part.

reviews.rationale: The hallucination part, and factual unreliability, are supported by April 2025 evaluations. The 'don't do much' part is contradicted by substantial coding-task success, though only on a developer-reported benchmark. The expense part is unresolved, because the packet has no operating-cost evidence. So the claim partly holds and partly fails.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'The punishment ... will be grim' is a firm forecast with no deadline. The normalised wording keeps the target (the tech industry) and the cause (betting on the AI bubble).

contract.note: The plain reading of 'grim' as severe, broad financial harm caused by AI investment is fair, given the surrounding text. The contract borrows source elements from the next sentence, but it judges 'grim' on breadth and severity without inventing a threshold.

evidence.note: Shows sharp falls in AI hardware and data-centre segments from 9 to 23 October 2026, but hyperscalers fell only 5.9%. The report also cites macro factors and position unwinds, so it falls short of the support condition.
Reuters reports a near-3% one-day fall in the Nasdaq amid AI-spending concerns. A short episode does not show grim punishment across the industry.
SaaS applications rose 4.6% over the same selloff, which weighs against broad damage so far. It does not contradict a forecast with no deadline.

reviews.rationale: There is no deadline. The October 2026 selloff was real but concentrated, partly attributed to macro factors and trading positions, and spared software applications. It is not the conclusive event of broad, severe, AI-attributable harm the contract requires, and time passing alone cannot contradict the claim. The evidence does not settle it.
